name: Freya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Freya, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say is confidential and won't be linked to your name. Can you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a city crew, so it's a mix of overhead lines in the older streets and underground cable in the newer bits. My day starts at seven at the east depot, and before that I've usually already asked an AI assistant to sort the fault reports from overnight and draft the job packs. Then it's traffic management, digging permits, angry shopkeepers whose power's off, and a joint to make in a hole in the pavement. I love solving a fault that's been dodging everyone for weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You use AI before you even get to the depot?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, on my phone over breakfast. It's brilliant for reading the network data and spotting a pattern, like one transformer tripping every time it rains. I also got my drone pilot licence last spring, paid for it myself, because I could see where inspections were heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a better clipboard, and that's fine. At work I'd probably get teased, because I'm the one always showing people new apps. Online I'd say the hype was overblown but the useful bits are worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a little bit disappointed? I was looking forward to drones and robots taking the dangerous jobs. But for my family it means no big shocks, and Mateo's teaching job and mine both stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, keep using the tools that help, and push the company to buy proper drones for inspections anyway. I'd keep the savings ticking over, we've got about two months' worth. Maybe I'd teach the crew a bit more of what I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the idea, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to get the assistant to read a fault log and tell you which pole to look at first. Amara, our cable jointer, thought it was a toy until it saved her a whole afternoon in the rain. Now she asks me for tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. What exactly would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to stop sending people into the worst jobs. I've pulled a mate out of a flooded cable pit, and I never want to do that again. If a robot could have gone in, I'd be thrilled.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out to be a better clipboard, and that's fine. Online I'd say the hype was overblown but the useful parts are worth keeping.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I wanted machines to take the dangerous jobs. For the family, it means no shocks and both our jobs stay put.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal while using the AI tools that help and pressing the company to buy inspection drones. Keeps the savings steady and teaches the crew more of what she uses.
S0.feel: Calm, slightly bored, a little let down.
S0.quote: If a robot could have gone in, I'd be thrilled.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is the rare worker who'd be disappointed by a plateau, because she hoped machines would take the dangerous work. The flooded cable pit story is behind that hope. She's already the crew's informal AI teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for the union to sit at the table, not stand outside it. The changes are coming either way, so let's make sure workers shape them and share the gains. I'd say that in a post and in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of it, and I feel a bit guilty saying that. I already know the tools and I've got the drone licence. The people I worry about are the ones who've never opened an app and don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to let me run a drone inspection trial in the first six months. I'd sign up for whatever robotics or network-data course they offered, and I'd help the union write a list of what training everyone should get. I'd ask for a pay grade for anyone running the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited even. With a bit of guilt mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you have in mind when you say people who don't want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lineman called Phil, twenty-five years in, best climber in the depot. He still prints out his job sheets. I'd want the union to make sure he isn't pushed out just because he doesn't like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say if you came home talking about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo would say, go on then, you've been waiting for this. He's a teacher, so he'd also ask who's teaching the Phils. He's usually right.

S1.say: I'd say the union should sit at the table, not stand outside it. Workers should shape the changes and share the gains.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of it because I know the tools and have a drone licence, and I feel guilty saying so. I worry about colleagues who avoid screens.
S1.do: Asks to run a drone inspection trial in the first six months and signs up for robotics or data courses. Helps the union draw up a training list and pushes for a pay grade for running new kit.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, with some guilt.
S1.quote: He still prints out his job sheets.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change suits Freya, and she knows it, which leaves her feeling guilty. She thinks about how others will manage, through the union, rather than only about herself. Her partner's question about who teaches the older workers clearly stays with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public plan, fast: income support, public ownership of the robots on the grid, and no one left to fall. I'd be campaigning, properly, not just posting. It's the electricity network, it belongs to everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think being good with AI buys me a year, maybe two, not a career. If the machines can do the whole job, my drone licence is just a nice certificate. We've only got two months saved and the mortgage is big because we bought near the ring road at the wrong time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up savings as hard as I can from day one, no holiday, no new car. I'd apply for any job managing robots on the network, at our company or the next one. And I'd join a campaign group, because two years is too short to fix this one family at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but my stomach's tight thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say campaigning, not just posting. What does that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going to meetings, standing up and speaking, knocking on doors if I have to. I did it once for a library closure in our area, with Iris on my shoulders. We lost that one, which is maybe why this scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids in that first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, but gently. Iris is thirteen and she'd read it all online anyway. Benji's eight, so I'd just tell him Mum's learning new things at work.

S2.say: I'd say we need a public plan, fast: income support, public ownership of robots on the grid, and no one left to fall. The network belongs to everyone.
S2.think: I think being good with AI buys me a year or two, not a career. With two months saved and a big mortgage, that worries me.
S2.do: Saves hard from day one, skipping the holiday and the new car. Applies for robot-management jobs at her company or a rival, and joins a campaign group.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight stomach, but not frozen.
S2.quote: If the machines can do the whole job, my drone licence is just a nice certificate.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-ready worker here admits her head start only buys time. Losing a library campaign shapes her fear that collective action can fail. Her response mixes personal job hunting with a strong push for public ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that every worker on the grid should be trained to run the new systems, and paid for it. I'd say the robots on a public network should be publicly owned. Same message, but less shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it a lot for me. I could become one of the people who maintains and supervises the robots, not one of the people they replace. That's a real job, and I think I'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd find a part-time course in robotics maintenance, probably two evenings a week at the technical college. I'd ask to move into the company's new technology team if it exists. And I'd stay on the union's training committee so the courses are open to everyone, not just people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two evenings a week with two kids and a crew to lead. How would that work at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo would do bedtime on those nights and I'd do weekends. We did the same when I got my diploma. It's tiring, but it's five years, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said what you'd do. What worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people around me, still. If only the keen ones move up, the depot splits in two. I don't want to be the boss of the robots while Phil's at home.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough to train and pay every grid worker to run the new systems. Robots on a public network should be publicly owned.
S3.think: I think five years lets me become someone who maintains and supervises the robots, not someone they replace. I'd be good at it.
S3.do: Starts a part-time robotics maintenance course two evenings a week and asks to move into the company's technology team. Stays on the union training committee to keep courses open to all.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, like a race she can run.
S3.quote: I don't want to be the boss of the robots while Phil's at home.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes a real difference for her: it's long enough to retrain into a supervising role. Her unease is mostly about fairness at the depot rather than her own income. She and her partner have a tried routine for studying around family life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. Shorter working weeks, training for everyone, and a public stake in the machines. I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is plenty. I'd be retrained well before 2036 and probably running a team that looks after robots. What worries me is whether governments use the time or just argue for nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan the retraining calmly over three or four years, and try to get the company to pay for it. I'd join a political party for the first time, because ten years is long enough for elections to matter. I'd also tell Iris to study what interests her, not what's safe, because nothing's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the country, calm about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell Iris nothing's safe. Does that feel strange to say to a thirteen-year-old?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. But I'd rather she hears it from me with a hug than from a news headline. She's tougher than I was at her age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra five years, compared to the last picture, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sleep better. With five years I'd be rushing and tired. With ten I could do it properly and still see Benji's school plays.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift we mustn't waste: shorter weeks, training for everyone and a public stake in the machines.
S4.think: I think ten years is plenty for me to retrain and run a team that maintains robots. I worry governments will argue for nine years and waste it.
S4.do: Plans retraining over three or four years, asking the company to pay. Joins a political party for the first time and encourages her daughter to study what interests her.
S4.feel: Calm about herself and uneasy about the country.
S4.quote: What worries me is whether governments use the time or just argue for nine years.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her personal worry almost disappears and her unease moves to politics. She'd join a party for the first time, which is a big step for her. She compares the five- and ten-year pictures mostly in terms of tiredness and family time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because nobody's ready, me included. What would help is free, paid-for training in running and fixing the robots, open to everyone on the grid, plus a basic income floor so families can keep their homes while they switch. And the public should own a share of what runs the network.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets to decide. I'm good with this stuff, and even I'd want a say in how it's used on my network. The people who climb the poles should be in the room.

headlineQuote: The people who climb the poles should be in the room.
portrait: Freya Torres is a 43-year-old city crew lead who works on both overhead lines and underground cable and uses AI tools every day. She paid for her own drone licence and would almost be disappointed if AI stalled, because she wants machines to take the dangerous jobs. She expects to do well from steady change, feels guilty about that, and worries about colleagues who avoid screens. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, since her head start only buys a year or two. With five or ten years she plans to retrain into maintaining and supervising robots, and her worry shifts to whether governments use the time well.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because nobody would be ready, including her.
whatWouldHelp: Free, paid training in running and fixing robots for everyone on the grid, a basic income floor so families keep their homes, and public ownership of a share of what runs the network.
